mcqs.question: What does it mean for gRPC's client/server code to 'enforce' the contract, compared to a REST API documented with OpenAPI?
options: Nothing different — OpenAPI documentation is exactly as enforced as generated gRPC code
gRPC has no contract at all, since it's purely binary
The generated client/server code is derived directly from the .proto schema, so a client literally cannot compile a call with a field the schema doesn't define
OpenAPI documentation is regenerated automatically whenever the REST server's code changes, making it equally enforced
mcqs.explanation: Because gRPC's client and server stubs are code-generated from the same .proto file, a mismatch becomes a compile-time error rather than a runtime surprise. OpenAPI docs are commonly hand-maintained or generated separately from the implementation and can drift silently — gRPC's generated code doesn't have that gap, and gRPC absolutely does define a contract (the .proto schema).

mcqs.question: A team retires a protobuf field, order_notes = 7, and later adds a brand-new field also using number 7 for a different type. What's the risk?
options: There's no risk — protobuf field numbers can always be safely reused once a field is no longer written
Old serialized data (or old clients) that encoded the original field 7 will be misinterpreted as the new field's type, silently corrupting data
This is disallowed by the compiler and will always fail to build
Field numbers only matter for performance, not for correctness
mcqs.explanation: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, not by name, so reusing a retired number for a different type means old data (or old clients still encoding it) gets decoded under the new field's type — a real, silent corruption risk. Most protobuf tooling won't catch this automatically unless the retired number is explicitly marked reserved, and it's very much a correctness issue, not just performance.

mcqs.question: A company is designing the public API that its own web app's browser JavaScript will call directly. Based on the compare slide, which should it lean toward?
options: gRPC, since it's always faster than REST/JSON regardless of the client
REST/JSON, since browsers speak it natively without an extra translation proxy
Either is equally suitable with no meaningful tradeoff for a browser client
Neither — browser-facing APIs should always use raw TCP sockets
mcqs.explanation: The compare slide is explicit that REST/JSON wins at the edge specifically because of native browser support — gRPC needs a gRPC-Web proxy for a browser to talk to it at all. gRPC's raw performance advantage doesn't help if the client can't speak the protocol without extra infrastructure, and raw TCP sockets aren't a realistic browser API mechanism.

mcqs.question: A team ships a public API meant to be called directly from browser JavaScript as raw gRPC, with no gateway or gRPC-Web proxy. What happens?
options: It works fine — modern browsers have native gRPC support built in
It works, but only in Chrome, since gRPC support varies by browser
Browsers cannot make the call at all — they can't set the HTTP/2 trailers gRPC relies on, and JavaScript has no native gRPC client
It works identically to a REST call since gRPC also runs over HTTP
mcqs.explanation: No mainstream browser has a native gRPC client or the ability to set the trailers gRPC's status mechanism depends on, so a direct call simply cannot be made — this isn't a partial or browser-specific limitation, it's universal. Running 'over HTTP' doesn't make it REST-compatible; the framing and semantics are fundamentally different.
